evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations throughout the manuscript (Alkhouli et al., 2020; Bunders and Altfeld, 2020; Gupta et al., 2021; Laxminarayan et al., 2020; Mauvais-Jarvis, 2020; O'Driscoll et al., 2021; Peckham et al., 2020; Richardson et al., 2020; Scully et al., 2020).

claim: The abundance of innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) decreases more than 7-fold over the human lifespan.
source: This observational study found that the abundance of innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) decreases more than 7-fold over the human lifespan – T cell subsets decrease less than 2-fold – and is lower in males than in females.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2A showing ILC abundance across age groups.

claim: T cell subsets decrease less than 2-fold over the human lifespan.
source: This observational study found that the abundance of innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) decreases more than 7-fold over the human lifespan – T cell subsets decrease less than 2-fold – and is lower in males than in females.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2A showing T cell abundance across age groups.

claim: ILC abundance is lower in males than in females.
source: This observational study found that the abundance of innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) decreases more than 7-fold over the human lifespan – T cell subsets decrease less than 2-fold – and is lower in males than in females.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2B and Table 2.

claim: After accounting for effects of age and sex, ILCs, but not T cells, were lower in adults hospitalized with COVID-19, independent of lymphopenia.
source: After accounting for effects of age and sex, ILCs, but not T cells, were lower in adults hospitalized with COVID-19, independent of lymphopenia.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by regression analysis in Table 2 and Figure 3.

claim: Among SARS-CoV-2-infected adults, the abundance of ILCs, but not of T cells, correlated inversely with odds of hospitalization.
source: Among SARS-CoV-2-infected adults, the abundance of ILCs, but not of T cells, correlated inversely with odds and duration of hospitalization, and with severity of inflammation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by logistic regression analysis in Table 3.

claim: Among SARS-CoV-2-infected adults, the abundance of ILCs correlated inversely with duration of hospitalization.
source: Among SARS-CoV-2-infected adults, the abundance of ILCs, but not of T cells, correlated inversely with odds and duration of hospitalization, and with severity of inflammation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by regression analysis in Table 4 and Figure 3C.

claim: Among SARS-CoV-2-infected adults, the abundance of ILCs correlated inversely with severity of inflammation.
source: Among SARS-CoV-2-infected adults, the abundance of ILCs, but not of T cells, correlated inversely with odds and duration of hospitalization, and with severity of inflammation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by regression analysis in Table 4 and Figure 3C showing inverse correlation with CRP and ESR.

claim: ILCs were uniquely decreased in pediatric COVID-19.
source: ILCs were also uniquely decreased in pediatric COVID-19 and the numbers of these cells did not recover during follow-up.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Table 5 and Figure 4A, B.

claim: ILC numbers did not recover during follow-up in pediatric COVID-19.
source: ILCs were also uniquely decreased in pediatric COVID-19 and the numbers of these cells did not recover during follow-up.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by longitudinal data in Figure 4D, E.

claim: Children with MIS-C had depletion of both ILCs and T cells.
source: In contrast, children with MIS-C had depletion of both ILCs and T cells, and both cell types increased during follow-up.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Table 5 and Figure 4A, B.

claim: Both ILCs and T cells increased during follow-up in children with MIS-C.
source: In contrast, children with MIS-C had depletion of both ILCs and T cells, and both cell types increased during follow-up.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by longitudinal data in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In both pediatric COVID-19 and MIS-C, ILC abundance correlated inversely with inflammation.
source: In both pediatric COVID-19 and MIS-C, ILC abundance correlated inversely with inflammation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Blood ILC mRNA tracked closely with ILCs from lung.
source: Blood ILC mRNA and phenotype tracked closely with ILCs from lung.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by RNA-Seq data in Figure 5 showing overlap in principal component analysis and shared gene expression patterns.

claim: Blood ILC phenotype tracked closely with ILCs from lung.
source: Blood ILC mRNA and phenotype tracked closely with ILCs from lung.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6A showing expression of TCF7 and CRTH2.

claim: Blood ILCs produced amphiregulin.
source: Importantly, blood ILCs produced amphiregulin, a protein implicated in disease tolerance and tissue homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6B showing AREG production after stimulation.

claim: Amphiregulin is a protein implicated in disease tolerance and tissue homeostasis.
source: Importantly, blood ILCs produced amphiregulin, a protein implicated in disease tolerance and tissue homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations (Branzk et al., 2018; Jamieson et al., 2013; Monticelli et al., 2015; Monticelli et al., 2011).

claim: Among controls, the percentage of ILCs that produced amphiregulin was higher in females than in males.
source: Among controls, the percentage of ILCs that produced amphiregulin was higher in females than in males, and people hospitalized with COVID-19 had a lower percentage of ILCs that produced amphiregulin than did controls.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 6C showing sex differences in AREG+ ILCs.

claim: People hospitalized with COVID-19 had a lower percentage of ILCs that produced amphiregulin than did controls.
source: Among controls, the percentage of ILCs that produced amphiregulin was higher in females than in males, and people hospitalized with COVID-19 had a lower percentage of ILCs that produced amphiregulin than did controls.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Lower ILC abundance contributes to increased COVID-19 severity with age.
source: These results suggest that, by promoting disease tolerance, homeostatic ILCs decrease morbidity and mortality associated with SARS-CoV-2 infection, and that lower ILC abundance contributes to increased COVID-19 severity with age and in males.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion drawn from the inverse correlation between ILC abundance and disease severity, combined with the age-related decline in ILCs.

claim: Lower ILC abundance contributes to increased COVID-19 severity in males.
source: These results suggest that, by promoting disease tolerance, homeostatic ILCs decrease morbidity and mortality associated with SARS-CoV-2 infection, and that lower ILC abundance contributes to increased COVID-19 severity with age and in males.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion drawn from the inverse correlation between ILC abundance and disease severity, combined with lower ILC abundance in males.

claim: Homeostatic ILCs decrease morbidity and mortality associated with SARS-CoV-2 infection by promoting disease tolerance.
source: These results suggest that, by promoting disease tolerance, homeostatic ILCs decrease morbidity and mortality associated with SARS-CoV-2 infection, and that lower ILC abundance contributes to increased COVID-19 severity with age and in males.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion based on the inverse correlation between ILC abundance and disease severity, and the known role of ILCs in disease tolerance from animal models.

claim: Among the hospitalized COVID-19 cohort, 82.5% were admitted to the ICU.

evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 1.

claim: Among the hospitalized COVID-19 cohort, 80% required intubation with mechanical ventilation.
source: The first group of blood donors in this study included SARS-CoV-2-infected adults hospitalized for severe COVID-19 (N = 40), among whom 33 (82.5%) were admitted to the ICU, 32 (80%) required intubation with mechanical ventilation, and 7 (17.5%) died (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 1.

claim: Among the hospitalized COVID-19 cohort, 17.5% died.
source: The first group of blood donors in this study included SARS-CoV-2-infected adults hospitalized for severe COVID-19 (N = 40), among whom 33 (82.5%) were admitted to the ICU, 32 (80%) required intubation with mechanical ventilation, and 7 (17.5%) died (Table 1).

claim: Differences in median age between hospitalized and outpatient COVID-19 groups were statistically significant (P = 5.2 x 10–8).

claim: Differences in sex ratio between hospitalized and outpatient COVID-19 groups were statistically significant (P = 3.7 x 10–3).
source: Differences between these two SARS-CoV-2-infected groups, in terms of median age (P = 5.2 x 10–8), sex ratio (P = 3.7 x 10–3), and diagnosis of diabetes mellitus (p = 1.05 x 10–3), were consistent with established risk factors for severe COVID-19 (Figure 1 and Table 1; Alkhouli et al., 2020; Bunders and Altfeld, 2020; Gupta et al., 2021; Laxminarayan et al., 2020; Mauvais-Jarvis, 2020; O'Driscoll et al., 2021; Peckham et al., 2020; Petrilli et al., 2020; Richardson et al., 2020; Scully et al., 2020).

evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 1.

claim: ILCs were the only lymphoid subset with significant differences among all age groups.
source: All cell types examined here were affected by age, but ILCs were the only subset with significant differences among all age groups, falling approximately twofold in median abundance every 20 years, with a greater than sevenfold decrease from the youngest to oldest age groups (p = 1.64 x 10–11) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ILC abundance falls approximately twofold in median abundance every 20 years.
source: All cell types examined here were affected by age, but ILCs were the only subset with significant differences among all age groups, falling approximately twofold in median abundance every 20 years, with a greater than sevenfold decrease from the youngest to oldest age groups (p = 1.64 x 10–11) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CD4+ T cells were less abundant in males than in females.
source: In addition, both ILCs and CD4+ T cells were less abundant in males (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: After accounting for effects of age and sex, individuals hospitalized with severe COVID-19 had 1.33-fold fewer total lymphocytes among PBMCs than did controls.
source: After accounting for effects of age and sex, individuals hospitalized with severe COVID-19 had 1.33-fold (95% CI: 1.49–1.19; p = 1.22 x 10–6) fewer total lymphocytes among PBMCs than did controls (Supplementary file 2d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by regression analysis in Supplementary file 2d.

claim: Lymphocyte abundance in people infected with SARS-CoV-2 who were treated as outpatients was not different from controls.
source: Lymphocyte abundance in people infected with SARS-CoV-2 who were treated as outpatients was not different from controls (Supplementary file 2d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by regression analysis in Supplementary file 2d.

source: In addition, total lymphocytes decreased with age and were less abundant in males (Supplementary file 2d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by regression analysis in Supplementary file 2d.

claim: Total lymphocytes were less abundant in males.
source: In addition, total lymphocytes decreased with age and were less abundant in males (Supplementary file 2d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by regression analysis in Supplementary file 2d.

claim: CD4+ T cells decreased with age across all three groups of adult blood donors.
source: Across all three groups of adult blood donors, CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, and ILCs decreased with age, while CD16+ NK cells increased with age, and both CD4+ T cells and ILCs were less abundant in males (Table 2 and Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 2 and Figure 3A.

claim: CD8+ T cells decreased with age across all three groups of adult blood donors.
source: Across all three groups of adult blood donors, CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, and ILCs decreased with age, while CD16+ NK cells increased with age, and both CD4+ T cells and ILCs were less abundant in males (Table 2 and Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 2 and Figure 3A.

claim: CD16+ NK cells increased with age across all three groups of adult blood donors.
source: Across all three groups of adult blood donors, CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, and ILCs decreased with age, while CD16+ NK cells increased with age, and both CD4+ T cells and ILCs were less abundant in males (Table 2 and Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 2 and Figure 3A.

claim: Adults hospitalized with COVID-19 had 1.78-fold fewer ILCs than controls when effects of age and sex were held constant.
source: When effects of age and sex were held constant, adults hospitalized with COVID-19 had 1.78-fold fewer ILCs (95% CI: 2.34–1.36; p = 4.55 x 10–5) and 2.31-fold fewer CD16+ natural killer (NK) cells (95% CI: 3.1–1.71; p = 1.04 x 10–7), as compared to controls (Table 2 and Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 2 and Figure 3B.

claim: Adults hospitalized with COVID-19 had 2.31-fold fewer CD16+ NK cells than controls when effects of age and sex were held constant.
source: When effects of age and sex were held constant, adults hospitalized with COVID-19 had 1.78-fold fewer ILCs (95% CI: 2.34–1.36; p = 4.55 x 10–5) and 2.31-fold fewer CD16+ natural killer (NK) cells (95% CI: 3.1–1.71; p = 1.04 x 10–7), as compared to controls (Table 2 and Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 2 and Figure 3B.

claim: Neither CD4+ T cells nor CD8+ T cells were depleted further than expected for age and sex in adults hospitalized with COVID-19.
source: Neither CD4+ T cells nor CD8+ T cells were depleted further than expected for age and sex (Table 2 and Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 2 and Figure 3B.

claim: SARS-CoV-2-infected adults treated as outpatients had 1.44-fold fewer CD16+ NK cells than controls.
source: As compared with controls, SARS-CoV-2-infected adults with less severe COVID-19 who were treated as outpatients had no reduction in ILCs, but 1.44-fold fewer CD16+ NK cells (95% CI: 1.93–1.07; p = 0.018), and 1.26-fold higher CD4+ T cells (95% CI: 1.06–1.5; p = 9.59 x 10–3) (Table 2 and Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 2 and Figure 3B.

claim: SARS-CoV-2-infected adults treated as outpatients had 1.26-fold higher CD4+ T cells than controls.
source: As compared with controls, SARS-CoV-2-infected adults with less severe COVID-19 who were treated as outpatients had no reduction in ILCs, but 1.44-fold fewer CD16+ NK cells (95% CI: 1.93–1.07; p = 0.018), and 1.26-fold higher CD4+ T cells (95% CI: 1.06–1.5; p = 9.59 x 10–3) (Table 2 and Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 2 and Figure 3B.

claim: SARS-CoV-2-infected adults treated as outpatients had no reduction in ILCs compared to controls.
source: As compared with controls, SARS-CoV-2-infected adults with less severe COVID-19 who were treated as outpatients had no reduction in ILCs, but 1.44-fold fewer CD16+ NK cells (95% CI: 1.93–1.07; p = 0.018), and 1.26-fold higher CD4+ T cells (95% CI: 1.06–1.5; p = 9.59 x 10–3) (Table 2 and Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 2 and Figure 3B.

claim: The adjusted odds ratio for hospitalization was 0.454 per twofold decrease in ILC abundance, representing a 54.6% increase in odds of hospitalization.
source: Abundance of ILCs, but not of CD16+ NK cells, CD4+ T cells, or CD8+ T cells was associated with odds of hospitalization: the odds ratio for hospitalization, adjusted for age, sex, diagnosis of diabetes mellitus, and symptom duration, was 0.454 (95%CI: 0.213–0.808; p = 0.018), an increase of 54.6% for each twofold decrease in ILC abundance (Table 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 3.

claim: Each twofold decrease in ILC abundance was associated with a 9.38-day increase in duration of hospital stay.
source: Holding age and sex constant, abundance of ILCs, but not of CD16+ NK cells, CD4+ T cells, or CD8+ T cells, was associated with length of time in the hospital: each twofold decrease in ILC abundance was associated with a 9.38-day increase in duration of hospital stay (95% CI: 15.76–3.01; p = 0.0054) (Figure 3C and Table 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 4 and Figure 3C.

claim: Each two-fold decrease in ILC abundance was associated with a 46.29 mg/L increase in blood CRP.
source: Holding age and sex constant, each two-fold decrease in ILC, but not in CD16+ NK cell, CD4+ T cell, or CD8+ T cell abundance, was associated with a 46.29 mg/L increase in blood CRP (95% CI: 71.34–21.24; p = 6.25 x 10–4) and 11.04 mm/hr increase in ESR (95% CI: 21.94–0.13; p = 0.047) (Figure 3C and Table 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 4 and Figure 3C.

claim: Each two-fold decrease in ILC abundance was associated with an 11.04 mm/hr increase in ESR.
source: Holding age and sex constant, each two-fold decrease in ILC, but not in CD16+ NK cell, CD4+ T cell, or CD8+ T cell abundance, was associated with a 46.29 mg/L increase in blood CRP (95% CI: 71.34–21.24; p = 6.25 x 10–4) and 11.04 mm/hr increase in ESR (95% CI: 21.94–0.13; p = 0.047) (Figure 3C and Table 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 4 and Figure 3C.

claim: Each two-fold decrease in ILC abundance was associated with an increase in D-dimer by 1098.52 ng/mL.
source: Abundance of both ILCs and CD4+ T cells was associated with blood levels of D-dimer, with each two-fold decrease in cell abundance associated with an increase in D-dimer by 1098.52 ng/mL (95% CI: 1932.84–264.19; p = 0.011) and 1868.85 ng/mL (95% CI: 3375.63–362.06; p = 0.016), respectively (Table 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 4.

claim: Each two-fold decrease in CD4+ T cell abundance was associated with an increase in D-dimer by 1868.85 ng/mL.
source: Abundance of both ILCs and CD4+ T cells was associated with blood levels of D-dimer, with each two-fold decrease in cell abundance associated with an increase in D-dimer by 1098.52 ng/mL (95% CI: 1932.84–264.19; p = 0.011) and 1868.85 ng/mL (95% CI: 3375.63–362.06; p = 0.016), respectively (Table 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 4.

claim: Blood ILCs in the pediatric cohort decreased with age.
source: Consistent with the findings in adults, blood ILCs in the pediatric cohort decreased with age (Table 5 and Figure 4A), demonstrating that the decrease in ILC abundance across the lifespan is already evident within the first two decades of life.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 5 and Figure 4A.

claim: Significant change over the pediatric age range was not detected in the abundance of CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, or CD16+ NK cells.
source: In contrast, significant change over this age range was not detected in the abundance of CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, or CD16+ NK cells (Table 5 and Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 5 and Figure 4A.

claim: Pediatric patients with COVID-19 had 1.69-fold fewer ILCs than controls after accounting for effects of age and sex.
source: After accounting for effects of age and sex, pediatric patients with COVID-19 had 1.69-fold fewer ILCs (95% CI: 2.73–1.04; p = 0.034) than controls (Figure 4A and Table 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 5 and Figure 4A.

claim: Neither CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, nor CD16+ NK cells were depleted in pediatric COVID-19 patients.
source: Neither CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, nor CD16+ NK cells were depleted in pediatric COVID-19 patients (Figure 4A and Table 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 5 and Figure 4A.

claim: Individuals with MIS-C had 2.14-fold fewer ILCs than controls.
source: As with pediatric COVID-19, ILCs were also lower in MIS-C, with 2.14-fold fewer ILCs (95% CI: 3.69–1.24; p = 0.007) than controls (Figure 4A and Table 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 5 and Figure 4A.

claim: Individuals with MIS-C had 1.6-fold fewer CD4+ T cells than pediatric controls.
source: However, unlike pediatric COVID-19, individuals with MIS-C had reduced numbers of T cells as compared with pediatric controls, with 1.6-fold fewer CD4+ T cells (95% CI: 2.04–1.26; p = 3.28 × 10–4) and 1.42-fold fewer CD8+ T cells (95% CI: 1.87–1.07; p = 0.016) (Figure 4A and Table 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 5 and Figure 4A.

claim: Individuals with MIS-C had 1.42-fold fewer CD8+ T cells than pediatric controls.
source: However, unlike pediatric COVID-19, individuals with MIS-C had reduced numbers of T cells as compared with pediatric controls, with 1.6-fold fewer CD4+ T cells (95% CI: 2.04–1.26; p = 3.28 × 10–4) and 1.42-fold fewer CD8+ T cells (95% CI: 1.87–1.07; p = 0.016) (Figure 4A and Table 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 5 and Figure 4A.

claim: Each twofold decrease in ILC abundance in pediatric patients hospitalized with COVID-19 or MIS-C was associated with a 40.5 mg/L increase in blood CRP.
source: Additionally, consistent with the finding in adults hospitalized with COVID-19 (Figure 3C and Table 4), after accounting for effect of group, each twofold decrease in ILC abundance in pediatric patients hospitalized with COVID-19 or MIS-C was associated with a 40.5 mg/L increase in blood CRP (95% CI: 77.87–3.13; p = 0.035) (Figure 4C), and no such association was detected with CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, or CD16+ NK cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Individuals recovering from MIS-C had a 2.39-fold increase in ILC abundance after accounting for effects of age, sex, and group.
source: After accounting for effects of age, sex, and group, individuals recovering from MIS-C had a 2.39-fold increase in ILC abundance (95% CI: 1.49–3.81; p = 6.6 × 10–3) but there was no significant change in ILC abundance for individuals recovering from COVID-19 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There was no significant change in ILC abundance for individuals recovering from COVID-19.
source: After accounting for effects of age, sex, and group, individuals recovering from MIS-C had a 2.39-fold increase in ILC abundance (95% CI: 1.49–3.81; p = 6.6 × 10–3) but there was no significant change in ILC abundance for individuals recovering from COVID-19 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Individuals recovering from MIS-C had 2.28-fold more ILCs than individuals recovering from COVID-19.
source: This analysis found no relationship between time to follow-up and abundance of any lymphoid subset, and that individuals recovering from MIS-C had 2.28-fold more ILCs (95% CI: 1.11–4.69; p = 0.0265) than individuals recovering from COVID-19 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: ILC abundance rebounded by 2 months of follow-up for MIS-C patients.
source: Of note, ILC abundance rebounded by 2 months of follow-up for the MIS-C patients, whereas ILC abundance still had not rebounded after 9 months of follow-up for the COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of follow-up data.

claim: ILC abundance had not rebounded after 9 months of follow-up for COVID-19 patients.
source: Of note, ILC abundance rebounded by 2 months of follow-up for the MIS-C patients, whereas ILC abundance still had not rebounded after 9 months of follow-up for the COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of follow-up data.

claim: Principal component analysis demonstrated overlap of blood ILCs with ILCs from the lung.
source: Unbiased principal component analysis demonstrated overlap of blood ILCs with ILCs from the lung, with clear separation from ILCs of jejunum or spleen origin (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 355 genes were consistently differentially expressed when either blood or lung ILCs were compared to ILCs from other tissues.
source: A total of 355 genes were consistently differentially expressed (fold-change >1.5, padj <0.01) when either blood or lung ILCs were compared to ILCs from the other tissues (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Genes significantly higher in both blood and lung ILCs included the ILC2-defining genes GATA3 and PTGDR2 (CRTH2).
source: Genes significantly higher in both blood and lung ILCs included the ILC2-defining genes GATA3 and PTGDR2 (CRTH2), as well as other genes important for ILC development such as TCF7 (Yang et al., 2013; Figure 5B and C).
